thread.title: Why Nvidia Is My Favorite Speculative Growth Name - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)

author: Nicholas Ward
title: Why Nvidia Is My Favorite Speculative Growth Name - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)
text:
It’s relatively rare that I invest in speculative growth stocks. While I acknowledge their vast potential for capital gains, I generally don’t have the stomach for their volatility and my value investing principles are too conservative to look so far into the future to justify prices paid in the present.
Recently, someone said that I invest like an old man. That’s okay though. Thankfully, my financial models show that I don’t have to take the risks that many younger investors do in pursuit of financial freedom. Investing like an old man for the next couple of decades should get me there. With that being said, I do have a handful of speculative, growth-oriented positions. In this piece, I’m going to discuss one of my favorite: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA ).
Capital preservation plays a large role in my investing philosophy. Usually, my reluctance to put invested capital at outsized risk puts me at odds with the high premiums investors must pay for growth names. Also, most speculative growth names don’t offer much in the way of a dividend and I have a difficult time justifying putting cash to work in the markets when it doesn’t work for me in return, contributing to my passive income stream.
But, with all of that being said, I have made some exceptions for high conviction growth plays. I think just about every portfolio should have a bit of exposure to the best in breed companies in secular growth industries. NVDA checks off several boxes in that regard, making it a relatively easy high premium name for me to own.
I’ve built a basket of speculative growth names (some of these names being more speculative than others). As you can see below, Nvidia is the second largest holding within this subset.
Company Ticker overall % of portfolio
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) 4.26% Nvidia (NVDA) 3.09% Amazon ( AMZN ) 1.69% Facebook ( FB ) 1.64% Alibaba ( BABA ) 1.49% Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ) 0.85% JD.com ( JD ) 0.70% Technology Select Sector SPDR ( XLK ) 0.44% The only weighting larger is Alphabet, which I include in this list even though its valuation actually isn’t all that speculative at less than 24x forward earnings. While I think it’s probably the most reliable name in this basket in terms of its moat, earnings, and cash flows, GOOGL is a part of my “speculative basket” because it doesn’t pay a dividend and trades with a fairly high TTM P/E ratio.
But even though GOOGL’s weighting is larger than NVDA’s, I’d probably say that NVDA is my growth name at the moment because of the relatively strong and unabated growth tailwinds behind it. The long-term strength of NVDA’s growth story isn’t unique, in my opinion, but I believe it does have relatively fewer headwinds/risks associated with it than many of its high growth peers.
Earlier in the year when market volatility picked up, I decided that it was time to re-risk my portfolio a bit. To do so, I trimmed a handful of growth names that had run up significant since my original purchases, locking in profits to bolster my cash position and add to more defensive, income-oriented positions (remember what I said about risk tolerance and the importance of capital preservation). However, I did not touch NVDA.
I’ve written before about why I think that Amazon has the longest growth runway in the entire market . I’ve said that Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) would be the first 1 trillion-dollar company, but if I had to guess, Amazon would be the first to make it to $2 trillion (with Alibaba running a close second in that race). However, both Amazon and Alibaba come with baggage that NVDA doesn’t.
I think NVDA’s long-term growth runway is nearly as attractive as AMZN’s and BABA’s, but NVDA has a much better valuation in term earnings than AMZN and doesn’t have the communist overhangs associated with BABA being domiciled in China. NVDA sits at an attractive intersection of probable long-term growth and not too terrible high premium multiple, trading for ~30.5x this year’s earnings. Amazon’s forward P/E ratio is nearly triple digits.
And, unlike the other domestic names in my growth basket Alphabet, Amazon, Facebook, NVDA doesn’t face legislative headwinds regarding privacy and anti-trust concerns. Chinese investments will always come with the inherent risk associated with communist China, lacking transparency, and concerns regarding questionable accounting. I’ve decided that the risk is worth the rewards when it comes to holding all of these names, but one of the primary reasons that I like NVDA so much is that, at the moment at least, neither the company’s primary growth drivers (the gaming industry and A.I./machine learnings/automation) face similar regulatory threats.
eSports NVDA is synonymous with eSports because of the performance of its graphics cards. Competitors will always want the best equipment when playing games and NVDA provides this. I know some will argue that Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) produces better chips, but from my perspective, NVDA remains on top here. Either way, I have no problem with owning shares of a company operating in an essential duopoly.
As more and more individuals become serious about games, demand for NVDA’s high end GPUs will continue to increase. And, on the lower end, consoles and computers that come with more baseline NVDA chips will continue to post strong sales volumes as well. This is good for NVDA, because in my opinion, there are fewer industries around that offer growth as reliable as video games.
One of the reasons that I expect for demand for gaming products to grow so reliably is eSports. As kids so many of us threw and kicked and bounced balls because of an attempt to be more like our athletic idols. Well, as we move further along into the digital age, these idols are changing. Believe it or not, eSports is producing celebrities. This trend has just begun and I think it’s far from over.
I know that watching digital games/competitions seems funny to some (if not most), but actually I’ve found that it’s really no different than watching any other show or sporting event on some sort of screen. Either way, you’re not present. Either way, you have no physical connection to the players in the match.
At first, I scoffed at the idea of eSports, but having gotten into playing/watching several games online, it really doesn’t feel any different to me from watching a football or basketball game. For the most part, the lives of professional athletes are fantasies, akin to the digital world of video game characters. It’s all about entertainment, either way.
And frankly put, eSports are a more efficient use of time, in my opinion. It takes hours to sit down and watch a football, baseball, basketball, etc., game from start to finish, whereas more video game matches last for 10-20 minutes. This could change as big business becomes increasingly involved in the eSports market, with professional leagues, etc, which will likely bring in advertisements.
However, I also suspect that the wealthy investors backing these teams/leagues understand the viewership dilemmas involving pace of play and ratings and hopefully they won’t make the same mistakes twice, hurting the quality of the entertainment product offered in lieu of a few extra dollars along the way. This is short-term thinking.
Also, while the games might not take place in the physical realm, there is still that real-life connection that makes video games seem so special. I grew up playing sports and therefore, I’ve always enjoyed watching the best of the best do things that I could only dream about. However, I also grew up playing video games and there will always be fantasy worlds and characters that elicit a nostalgic response from me.
Well, in a world where more and more kids play video games on a regular basis, this nostalgic response is only growing stronger. I think that kids should get outside and play a bit more. A sedentary lifestyle is hazardous to human health. However, as gaming experiences and graphics continue to improve, I think the “realness” of these digital worlds/games will continue to take market share from traditional sports/games/play time.
Am I saying that I will stop watching real life sports? No. But, I can definitely see the allure of eSports and I suspect that over the long-term, their popularity will continue to grow, both for me personally, and for the broader public, as well.
A.I./Robotics It’s scary to consider a more automated future. You’ve got Elon Musk calling A.I. the devil. Stephen Hawking talked about A.I.’s potential to bring about Armageddon. Many others much smarter than me have brought up similar concerns. As a layperson, my mind goes to the Terminator movies… science fiction has turned into reality many times before and I fear a future run by Skynet.
Granted, it’s also worth noting that many other genius level minds have come out on the other side of the A.I. fence, praising its ability to contribute to human society in a myriad of ways. I suppose only time will tell what the future holds with regard to singularity.
Maybe my fears are unfounded. Who knows. Before I mentioned the lack of regulatory/legislative headwinds for NVDA, this could change if sentiment towards A.I. changes and it becomes an obvious threat to the public. However, I think we’re far from that point and it seems to me like most people are siding on the side of convenience rather than caution. My personal fears aside, the way I see it, we’re headed down the path towards widespread A.I./robotics and I’ve decided to go with the “if you can’t be them, join them” mindset, investing in companies like NVDA.
NVDA has been a leader in the A.I./machine learning space for quite some time now and assuming that these robots don’t revolt and kill us all one day, I imagine investors who’ve gotten in early with NVDA on this trend will be rewarded heavily in financial terms.
In a recent piece written here at SA by Mark Hibben , he brought up ~$30b estimates regarding collaborative and commercial robotics ~5 years out. As investments in automation lead to more productivity and fewer costs, I suspect that CEOs across the sector/industry spectrums will continue to automate their operations
Longer term, as 5G is ushered in, it’s likely that we’ll enter another industrial revolution centered around big data/automation. Everything from toasters to cars are already becoming “intelligent” and as latency decreases in the wireless transmission of data, more and more machines will be deemed “smart.”
NVDA should be one of the big winners of this trend and while I do have broader societal concerns regarding job loss and unskilled workers being left behind, I don’t doubt that productivity will trump these potential costs and I’m happy to be in a position to potentially benefit from this trend as a shareholder. As a relatively low-skilled worker myself (I could imagine a day where most financial analysis is done by machines), I view my relatively large position in NVDA as a means of hedging my bets a bit in terms of my chosen profession.
Fundamentals Since the start of 2015, NVDA is on an amazing run. Shares have increased more than ten-fold, from ~$20 to ~$250. Unfortunately for me, I wasn’t involved in the first couple of years of this run. However, I did enter into NVDA stock at the beginning of 2017. I made two purchases at $110 and $117 in January and February of 2017. I can’t claim a 10-bagger here (yet), but I also can’t complain about my gains and the results NVDA has produced since my purchase.
Because of NVDA’s high premiums, there is oftentimes a lot of short-term noise surrounding this company. I hear about GPU delays, supply issues, demand issues, competitors gaining traction, innovative systems failing, government regulation getting in the way, etc. I get it, when a company is essentially priced to perfection, the market, and especially short-term investors, get worried. However, I think it makes more sense to take a long-term view with a potentially revolutionary company like NVDA and ignore most, if not all of this news, and simply trusting in this management team to continue to deliver into the future just as it has in the past.
NVDA’s soaring share price didn’t happen by accident. Since 2014, NVDA’s revenues have more than doubled while its EPS has improved from $0.74/share to $4.82/share. Operating cash flows are up from $835m to $3.5b during the last 5 years. Margins have increased, outstanding share count has remained relatively steady (up 6.7% over the last 5 years), and long-term debt remains low. NVDA still trades with a speculative, forward-looking valuation, but there are positive fundamentals to give a base to this stock.
NVDA’s share price consolidation since January has helped the company’s valuation as well. NVDA began the year in the $250 range and after a bit of fluctuations, remains there today. However, since this stock’s earnings are growing so quickly, the P/E ratio has fallen significantly in a relatively short period of time. NVDA began the year with a TTM P/E ratio of ~50x and now that multiple sits at ~40x. Analysts expect to see ~60% EPS growth in 2019. This level of growth obviously isn’t sustainable, but looking out further ahead, analysts still expect to see double-digit growth from NVDA.
I think a ~30x TTM multiple is acceptable for a company with these sort of growth characteristics. Assuming current growth estimates hold true, even if NVDA’s multiple contracts from the ~40x range to the ~30x range, we’re looking at a ~$300 share price in January of 2021. If multiples don’t contract and/or management produces growth that is higher than expectations, then this share price figure could be much, much higher. And, considering the fact that NVDA has beaten analysts' estimates for 11 consecutive quarters, I’d say that chances are likely that 2021 estimate is a tad too low.
The Dividend And lastly, although NVDA doesn’t do much to contribute to my passive income stream because of its low dividend yield (0.25%), that might not always be the case. NVDA has provided investors with strong, double-digit dividend growth every year since initiating its payments in 2013. NVDA has a near single-digit payout ratio, so I see no reason why that double-digit dividend growth can’t continue. Obviously, a stock with such a low yield probably isn’t right for income-oriented investors with relatively short investment horizons; however, for a young man like myself, I think NVDA could be a passive cash flow machine in a couple of decades.
Only time will tell, but I’m happy to partner with this revolutionary company as a shareholder while I wait. There are very few companies with TTM multiples in the 40x range that I consider to be S.W.A.N. (sleep well at night) type holdings. Heck, there are very few with multiples above 20x. But, NVDA is one of them.
Disclosure: I am/we are long NVDA, AMZN, GOOGL, FB, BABA, TCEHY, JD, XLK.
